extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and other practitioners who appear before the USPTO (respondents in disciplinary/reciprocal-discipline matters) and USPTO/OED staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedures, and examples governing imposition of reciprocal discipline by the USPTO under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 (including the Selling v. Radford factors, burden of proof, response procedure, sanctions, probation/reinstatement, and examples of misconduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d) — factors to avoid reciprocal discipline (Selling elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process; (ii) There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject; (iii) The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice; or (iv) Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four Selling-derived factors are the sole bases listed in § 11.24(d) to prevent imposition of identical reciprocal discipline. The practitioner must raise a genuine issue of material fact as to at least one factor by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the imposition of reciprocal discipline, Respondent is required to demonstrate that she meets one of the factors in 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d) by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts and the Office place the burden on the respondent; the standard is narrow and particularly difficult where the respondent stipulated to facts and violations. The USPTO does not sit to re‑weigh the state court's findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling v. Radford presumption and limited review
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Selling v. Radford, state disbarment creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper unless one of the Selling elements is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO's review is 'extremely limited' and not a de novo review — it looks only for the kind of infirmities identified in Selling (due process failure, infirmity of proof, grave injustice, or lack of public discipline).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) — conduct reflecting adversely on fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10.23(b)(6) provides that '[a] practitioner shall not ... [e]ngage in any conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding by a state authority that a practitioner engaged in such conduct (e.g., suspension on ethical grounds) supports imposition of reciprocal discipline under § 11.24 unless the Selling factors are shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of reciprocal discipline — not limited to patent/trademark matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.24 requires reciprocal discipline when a practitioner before the Office is censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred or suspended by another jurisdiction; the plain language does not restrict reciprocal discipline only to matters where the original discipline occurred in connection with a patent or trademark matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the underlying misconduct occurred in non‑patent practice (e.g., mortgage matters) or involved Office matters in whole/part does not preclude reciprocal discipline so long as the practitioner is subject to discipline by another jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: California Rule 3-110(A) — competence (as applied here)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 3-110(A) proscribes 'intentionally, recklessly, or repeatedly failing to perform legal services with competence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in this matter to findings that Respondent: (i) failed to obtain loan modifications or perform other legal services of value for seven clients; (ii) failed to respond to a Notice of Missing Parts and other correspondence from the USPTO causing clients' patent applications to become abandoned; and (iii) failed to forward an issue fee to the USPTO causing a patent application to become abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: California Rule 3-700(D)(2) — refund of unearned fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 3-700(D)(2) requires, in part, that a member whose employment has terminated shall promptly refund any part of a fee paid in advance that has not been earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied here to findings that Respondent failed to promptly refund fees paid in advance for legal services and fees paid to cover an issue fee despite not having forwarded the fee to the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure — Notice and 40-day response requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deputy General Counsel for General Law, on behalf of the USPTO Director, issued a Notice and Order Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 giving Respondent forty days to file a response 'containing all information that Respondent believes is sufficient to establish a genuine issue of material fact that the imposition of discipline identical to that imposed by the California Supreme Court would be unwarranted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must timely present all evidence and arguments within that period; failure to do so limits ability to show a genuine issue of material fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: No entitlement to de novo review
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no entitlement to a de novo review; the Office need only 'determine whether the record underlying the predicate state disbarment reveals the kind of infirmities identified in Selling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of review is narrow; courts have described it as extremely limited and not an opportunity to re-litigate the underlying facts or substitute the Office's judgment for the state tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement eligibility under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent may request reinstatement pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 after serving six months of her one-year USPTO suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reinstatement is granted, the respondent may be permitted to practice trademark and other non-patent law before the USPTO during the remainder of the probationary period provided she satisfies the conditions of 37 C.F.R. § 11.14(a) and is not subsequently suspended or excluded from practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation enforcement — Order to Show Cause and immediate suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: If the OED Director believes Respondent fails to comply with any provision of the Final Order or any Disciplinary Rule during the two-year probationary period, the OED Director may: (a) issue an Order to Show Cause why the USPTO Director should not order immediate suspension for up to an additional six months; (b) send the Order to Show Cause to Respondent where OED reasonably believes Respondent receives mail; and (c) grant Respondent fifteen (15) days to respond to the Order to Show Cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the response period, the OED Director may deliver the Order to Show Cause, Respondent's response, and argument/evidence to the USPTO Director and request immediate additional suspension up to six months. Alternatively, if Respondent has not been reinstated, OED may consider alleged failures in connection with a reinstatement request or pursue discipline under 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.34–11.57.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of notice of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall make public the following Notice in the Official Gazette: (example Notice of Suspension describing the discipline, basis, relevant rules violated, and a statement regarding patent-practitioner status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary actions involving practitioners are also posted for public reading at the OED Reading Room (URL provided in the Order). The Notice must identify the practitioner, the discipline imposed, the rule(s) violated, and relevant factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of factual misconduct that support adverse fitness finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific factual findings supporting ethical violations included: failing to obtain loan modifications or perform legal services of value for seven clients; failing to respond to correspondence from the USPTO causing patent applications to become abandoned; failing to forward an issue fee causing an application to become abandoned; failing to promptly refund fees paid in advance for legal services or for an issue fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete examples illustrate the kinds of conduct that may be found to 'adversely reflect on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office' and can underlie reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner status definitions (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.14(a), 11.19(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no question that Respondent is a practitioner before the Office in that she was an attorney in good standing who was engaged in practice before the Office (citing 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.14(a), 11.19(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal discipline under § 11.24 applies to persons who meet the regulatory definitions of practitioners before the USPTO, even if they are not registered patent practitioners authorized to practice patent law before the Office.
